initial_requirements: Vrije Universiteit Brussel needs a Publications Management System for storing bibliographic records and full publication texts. Users with different roles should be able to search, upload, download, correct, and moderate publication information according to their access rights. The system should extract bibliographic details from documents, support bulk imports, and help reconcile alternative names that refer to the same author or institution.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you describe the different user roles involved in the Publications Management System and the main actions each role should be allowed to perform, especially for searching, uploading, correcting, moderating, and downloading publication records?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, at a high level we expect a few different roles. Regular researchers or staff should mainly be able to search the publications, upload new records or full texts for their own work, and download records or documents they have access to. Editors or faculty admins would have broader rights to correct metadata, merge duplicates, and review uploads before they become visible more widely. Then there should be moderators or librarians who can approve, reject, or adjust publication information, handle exceptions, and manage author or institution name reconciliation. I’m not fully sure yet where the boundary should be between faculty admins and central library staff, so that part would need confirmation.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you define the access control model in more detail—for each role, what specific permissions should they have for viewing, uploading, editing, approving, rejecting, merging, and handling publication records, and are there any rules based on ownership, faculty, or publication status?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
We’d want access to be tied both to role and to the scope of the record. In general, authors or contributors can view all public records and edit only the items they own or submitted, while faculty admins can edit records within their faculty and approve routine changes. Moderators or librarians should have the highest operational rights: they can approve, reject, merge duplicate records, and correct metadata across faculties when needed.
Ownership matters for draft or newly uploaded records, because the submitter should be able to revise them until they are approved. Once a record is published or approved, normal users shouldn’t overwrite it directly; they should create a correction request or a new version depending on the workflow. I’d also expect some status-based rules, like drafts being visible only to the owner and reviewers, approved records being broadly searchable, and rejected records staying hidden except for audit purposes.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you describe the publication status lifecycle you want the system to support—for example, the possible statuses a record should move through from draft or upload through review, approval, publication, rejection, correction, or replacement, and what triggers each transition?
turns.interviewee_utterance: We’d need a simple lifecycle with a draft or imported state first, where the record is created but not yet validated. Then it should move into review once a user submits it or a bulk import is processed, and at that point a moderator or librarian can either approve it, send it back for correction, or reject it if it is wrong or incomplete. Approved records become published and searchable for everyone with access, and if later corrections are needed, I’d expect either an updated version to replace the old one or a correction status that keeps the history. If a publication is superseded by a newer version, the old one should probably be marked as replaced rather than deleted, so we keep traceability.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When publications are brought in through bulk import or automatic bibliographic extraction, what validation checks should the system perform before a record is accepted—for example, required fields, format checks, duplicate detection, confidence thresholds, and whether low-quality or uncertain items should be rejected, queued for review, or routed to a specific role?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Before accepting an imported record, the system should check that the core bibliographic fields are present and valid, things like title, authors, year, and at least one identifier if available. It should also do format checks on dates, DOI or ISBN patterns, file types for uploads, and basic consistency between the extracted text and the metadata. Duplicate detection is important too, especially against existing records and alternative author or institution names.
For extraction confidence, I’d expect a threshold rule. High-confidence items could go straight into the review queue or even be auto-accepted for very simple cases, while low-confidence or incomplete records should not be published automatically and should go to a moderator or librarian for manual checking. If the quality is too poor, the system should reject the item or flag it as unusable rather than letting it clutter the database.

slots.name: project_goals
slots.value: Provide a Publications Management System for storing bibliographic records and full publication texts, supporting search, upload, download, correction, moderation, bulk import, and reconciliation of alternative author or institution names.

slots.name: stakeholder_roles
slots.value: Regular researchers or staff; editors or faculty admins; moderators or librarians; central library staff (boundary with faculty admins still to be confirmed).

slots.name: functional_needs
slots.value: Users must be able to search publications, upload new records or full texts, download accessible records/documents, correct metadata, merge duplicates, review uploads before publication, approve/reject/adjust publication information, handle exceptions, and reconcile alternative author or institution names.

slots.name: business_rules
slots.value: Access is tied to both role and record scope: authors/contributors can view all public records and edit only items they own or submitted; faculty admins can edit records within their faculty and approve routine changes; moderators/librarians have highest operational rights to approve, reject, merge duplicate records, and correct metadata across faculties. Ownership governs draft or newly uploaded records, and once a record is approved/published, normal users cannot overwrite it directly.

slots.name: data_entities
slots.value: Publication records, full publication texts, bibliographic metadata, duplicate records, author names, institution names, draft/newly uploaded records, approved/published records, rejected records, and correction requests or new versions.

slots.name: constraints
slots.value: The exact boundary of responsibility between faculty admins and central library staff is not yet confirmed.

slots.name: quality_concerns
slots.value: Imported records must have core bibliographic fields present and valid; date, DOI/ISBN, and file format checks are required; metadata should be consistent with extracted text; low-confidence or poor-quality imports must not be auto-published and may be routed for manual review or rejected as unusable.

slots.name: boundary_conditions
slots.value: Need confirmation on where responsibility ends for faculty admins and begins for central library staff.

slots.name: access_control_model
slots.value: Role-based and scope-based access control. Authors/contributors can view public records and edit only owned or submitted items. Faculty admins can edit records within their faculty and approve routine changes. Moderators/librarians have broader cross-faculty rights to approve, reject, merge duplicates, and correct metadata. Drafts are visible only to the owner and reviewers; approved records are broadly searchable; rejected records are hidden except for audit purposes.

slots.name: publication_visibility_rules
slots.value: Draft records are visible only to the owner and reviewers. Approved or published records are broadly searchable. Rejected records remain hidden except for audit purposes.

slots.name: name_reconciliation_workflow
slots.value: Moderators or librarians handle reconciliation of alternative author or institution names as part of publication review and metadata correction, including cross-faculty corrections when needed.

slots.name: duplicate_resolution_policy
slots.value: Faculty admins can merge duplicates within their scope, while moderators or librarians can merge duplicate records across faculties and during approval or correction workflows.

slots.name: moderation_exception_handling
slots.value: Moderators or librarians can approve, reject, or adjust publication information and handle exceptions; normal users must use correction requests or new versions instead of overwriting approved records.

slots.name: publication_status_lifecycle
slots.value: A simple lifecycle is required: draft/imported, then review when a user submits a record or a bulk import is processed, then approved/published, rejected, corrected, or replaced. Moderators or librarians can approve, send back for correction, or reject records during review. If corrections are needed after publication, the system should support either a new version or a correction status that preserves history. Superseded publications should be marked as replaced rather than deleted to maintain traceability.

slots.name: versioning_and_correction_requests
slots.value: If an approved record needs changes, users should not overwrite it directly; they should submit a correction request or create a new version. Updated versions may replace older ones, while history should be preserved. Replaced records should remain traceable rather than deleted.

slots.name: audit_and_retention_rules
slots.value: Superseded publications should be marked as replaced rather than deleted so traceability is preserved. Rejected records remain hidden except for audit purposes.

slots.name: search_and_discovery_requirements
slots.value: Approved records should be broadly searchable; draft records are restricted to owner/reviewers, and rejected records are not searchable except for audit purposes.

slots.name: bulk_import_validation_rules
slots.value: Bulk/imported records must be checked for required bibliographic fields such as title, authors, year, and at least one identifier if available; format checks should validate dates, DOI/ISBN patterns, file types, and consistency between extracted text and metadata. High-confidence items may proceed to review or be auto-accepted in simple cases, while low-confidence or incomplete records should be routed to manual review or rejected if quality is too poor.

slots.name: bibliographic_extraction_confidence_handling
slots.value: Extraction should use a confidence threshold: high-confidence items may go to the review queue or be auto-accepted in simple cases, while low-confidence or incomplete records must not be published automatically and should be sent to a moderator or librarian for manual checking.

slots.name: import_duplicate_detection
slots.value: Duplicate detection is required during imports and should check both existing records and alternative author or institution names.

slots.name: import_exception_routing
slots.value: Low-confidence, incomplete, or poor-quality imported records should be routed to a moderator or librarian for manual checking; if the quality is too poor, the item should be rejected or flagged as unusable rather than published.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The system must support bulk imports and automatic extraction of bibliographic details from documents, but the dialogue has not yet clarified how imported or extracted metadata should be validated, de-duplicated, or routed when quality is uncertain.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely reflects a need to minimize manual cataloging effort while still protecting metadata quality, so the system may require explicit import validation, confidence handling for extraction, and exception routing before records become publicly searchable.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The workflow now includes post-publication corrections and version replacement, but the dialogue has not clarified how the system should preserve traceability across changes, rejections, and replaced publications over time.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely reflects a repository-oriented institutional need for auditability and scholarly provenance, where publication history must remain reconstructable for accountability, citation integrity, and administrative review, so explicit rules for version history, change tracking, and retention need to be captured.
